The strongest case for remote becoming the default rests on four claims that have actually held up under several years of evidence.

For workers, remote work removes the commute, which for many people is the single largest unwaged drain on their week — easily ten to fifteen hours plus several thousand dollars a year. It widens the geographic labor market, so people can take a job in an expensive city without paying its rent. It lets caregivers, disabled workers, and people in two-career households arrange their lives in ways the standard office actively prevented. Self-reported wellbeing rises, attrition falls in surveys, and most knowledge workers given the choice take some remote mix.

For managers and firms, the visible win is real-estate cost; the less visible one is access to talent outside a handful of expensive metros. There's also evidence that focused individual work — the kind that needs blocks of uninterrupted attention — happens more easily at home than in an open office. Hybrid in particular has emerged as a stable equilibrium where teams retain some in-person collaboration without the daily commute tax.

For cities, remote work redistributes economic activity from downtown lunch spots to neighborhood ones. Smaller and mid-sized cities benefit when residents who would have moved to expensive coastal hubs stay put with high-paying jobs. Climate and traffic externalities of long commutes are reduced.

The strongest case against making it the default also rests on four claims worth taking seriously.

The new-employee problem is the deepest one. Onboarding, mentorship, and absorbing a workplace's tacit norms turn out to be much harder over video. Junior staff in fully remote roles report weaker peer networks, slower skill growth, and lower visibility for promotion. Several years in, those costs compound: people who started remote may be structurally disadvantaged compared to peers who got in-person apprenticeship time. Defaulting to remote risks pulling up the ladder behind the people who built their careers in offices.

The collaboration-quality argument is harder to measure but recurs across industries. Some kinds of work — early-stage product brainstorming, debugging tense team dynamics, building trust on cross-functional projects — seem to benefit from physical co-presence in ways video does not fully replicate. Companies that went fully remote often report a creeping decline in the kinds of conversations that don't happen on a calendar.

For managers, remote work makes performance harder to read and culture harder to transmit. Some respond with more measurement (surveillance software, output metrics) which often makes things worse. Others quietly select for self-managers, which advantages people already good at remote work and disadvantages everyone else.

For cities, the case against remote default is that office districts are anchor economies, and rapid remote shifts have hollowed out commercial cores faster than tax bases can adjust, with real consequences for transit, retail, and city services.

A fair synthesis is that fully-in-office and fully-remote are both extreme positions; the live debate is really about hybrid ratios, the threshold below which the new-employee and collaboration costs become serious, and whether the gains from remote work can be preserved while building structures (returnships, intentional onboarding cohorts, periodic in-person weeks) that protect early-career workers. The answer probably differs by industry, role, and seniority more than by ideology.
